extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IP lawyers, law students, and legal scholars interested in inducement doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether a defendant can be held liable for induced infringement under the Federal Circuit's Akamai decision, focusing on proof of specific intent and the use of circumstantial evidence. Emphasizes factors courts should weigh when infringement is collective (no single actor performs all steps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific intent to induce infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Akamai still requires the alleged inducer to have the specific intent to induce infringement (Akamai, 692 F.3d at 1308).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even after Akamai expanded circumstances in which liability may be found, the patent owner must provide evidence—direct or circumstantial—showing the defendant possessed the specific intent to induce infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of circumstantial evidence to prove intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct evidence of inducement is often hard to come by, so patent owners must often resort to circumstantial evidence to prove specific intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should weigh circumstantial evidence carefully, particularly in cases of collective or divided infringement where no single actor performed all method steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus (one of Gross's three factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nexus is one of three factors Mr. Roy D. Gross recommends courts weigh when determining whether circumstantial evidence establishes the requisite intent to induce infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether there is a sufficient connection between the alleged inducer's actions and the infringing acts to support an inference of intent; the article recommends weighing this alongside control and mitigating evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control (one of Gross's three factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Control is another factor Gross recommends courts consider when evaluating circumstantial evidence of intent to induce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the alleged inducer exercised control over the actors who performed the infringing steps (e.g., through instructions, instructions' necessity, or direction), which supports an inference of intent to induce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating evidence of intent not to infringe (one of Gross's three factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating evidence that the alleged inducer intended not to infringe is the third factor Gross recommends courts weigh in evaluating circumstantial evidence of specific intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence demonstrating steps taken to avoid infringement or a lack of intent to encourage infringement should be considered and can negate an inference of specific intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Akamai's effect on divided performance liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Akamai arguably made it easier for patent owners to hold a person liable for induced infringement of a method claim when no single person performed all the steps of the method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Akamai allows suits against those who induced collective infringement, litigators and courts must still grapple with how to weigh circumstantial evidence of intent in these more strained scenarios; understanding and applying the nexus/control/mitigating-evidence framework can help close the prior loophole without abandoning the specific-intent requirement.
